cards.title: DBMS Architecture — The Four Major Subsystems
cards.teaser: Every database management system — from SQLite to Postgres to CockroachDB — is built from four interacting subsystems. Understanding how they interact is the prerequisite for understanding any engine-level behavior.

runs.text: Strip away the SQL dialect and the configuration knobs and you find the same four-subsystem architecture in virtually every relational DBMS:

items.text: — manages files, pages, and the physical layout of data on disk. It is the only subsystem that talks to the operating system's I/O layer directly.
— the page cache between disk and all in-memory processing. Loads pages on demand, evicts cold pages, tracks dirty pages awaiting write-back.
— enforces ACID properties. Composed of a transaction manager (BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK lifecycle), a lock manager (concurrency isolation), and a recovery manager (crash safety via the WAL).
— converts SQL text into an execution plan and runs it. Composed of the parser, planner, optimizer, and executor.

runs.text: The subsystems are not merely layered — they are tightly coupled. The query executor calls into the transaction subsystem to acquire locks before touching pages. The transaction subsystem calls into the buffer pool to fetch and pin pages. The buffer pool calls into the storage subsystem to issue block reads. Every database bug at scale traces back to an interaction across one of these seams.

Petrov's Database Internals (O'Reilly, 2019) uses this four-subsystem decomposition as its organizing principle. The CMU 15-445/645 course (Andy Pavlo) breaks the architecture the same way, calling them Storage, Execution, Concurrency Control, and Recovery — different names, same structure.

Every database is built from four subsystems: storage (files on disk), buffer pool (page cache in RAM), transactions (ACID enforcement), and query processing (SQL → plan → results). Each one calls the one below it.

cards.title: Storage Subsystem — Disk Layer Responsibilities
cards.teaser: The storage subsystem is the only part of a DBMS that knows about files and physical disk layout. Everything above it works with pages — fixed-size byte arrays — and expects the storage layer to make those pages durable.

runs.text: The storage subsystem is responsible for five concrete tasks:

items.text: Data is organized into fixed-size pages — typically 4 KB, 8 KB, or 16 KB. Postgres uses 8 KB pages; InnoDB uses 16 KB; SQLite uses configurable page sizes from 512 B to 65 KB. Every heap tuple, every B-tree node, every WAL record maps to one or more pages. The page is the atomic unit of I/O.

Tables and indexes are stored in segment files (Postgres) or tablespace files (InnoDB). The storage engine manages the mapping from logical page IDs to physical file offsets, and expands segment files as tables grow.

When rows are deleted or updated, their former space must be tracked and reused. Postgres maintains a Free Space Map (FSM) per relation — a space-efficient structure recording available space per page. Without FSM, deleted space would never be reclaimed without a full VACUUM rewrite.

The storage layer is responsible for fsync semantics — ensuring WAL records reach durable storage before the transaction manager declares a commit. The correctness guarantee: WAL data must hit disk before the corresponding data pages do (write-ahead property). Violating this leads to unrecoverable data loss on crash.

On modern SSDs and spinning disks, a partial page write (torn page) can silently corrupt data. Postgres data checksums (enabled at initdb time) compute a CRC-32 over each page; mismatches on read surface corruption before it propagates. SQLite uses a similar mechanism on WAL journal pages.

runs.text: Crucially, the storage subsystem does
not

decide which pages to keep in memory — that is the buffer pool's job. It does not decide transaction ordering — that is the transaction manager's job. Its contract is precisely defined: read page N from file F, write page N to file F, fsync WAL, report corruption.

The storage subsystem owns the physical layout: how data maps to fixed-size pages, how pages map to files, how deleted space gets tracked, and how the WAL gets persisted. Everything above it works in terms of page IDs and trusts this layer to make those pages real and durable.

cards.title: Transaction Subsystem — Txn Manager, Lock Manager, Recovery Manager
cards.teaser: The transaction subsystem is the conscience of the database — it is what makes reads and writes appear atomic, isolated, and durable. Three collaborating managers divide this responsibility.

runs.text: ACID properties do not fall out of storage layout — they require active enforcement at runtime. The transaction subsystem provides that enforcement through three collaborating components:

items.text: Manages transaction lifecycle: BEGIN allocates a transaction ID (XID in Postgres; trx_id in InnoDB), COMMIT persists the transaction's changes and makes them visible to other transactions, ROLLBACK undoes in-flight changes using undo log records. The transaction manager must coordinate with the recovery manager so that committed transactions survive crashes and aborted transactions are unwound.

Enforces isolation by controlling concurrent access to shared data. In a two-phase locking (2PL) system, transactions acquire locks before accessing rows and release them only at commit or abort. Lock managers maintain a lock table mapping resources (row IDs, page IDs, table OIDs) to lock holders and waiters. Deadlock detection is a secondary responsibility — the lock manager must periodically inspect the waiter graph and abort a victim transaction to break cycles. Postgres uses a combination of 2PL and MVCC; InnoDB uses 2PL with row-level gap locks to prevent phantom reads.
Maintains the write-ahead log (WAL) and implements the ARIES algorithm (Mohan et al., 1992) for crash recovery. ARIES has three phases:
(scan the WAL to determine which transactions were active at crash),
(reapply all logged changes to restore the database to the exact state at crash, including dirty pages of uncommitted transactions),
(roll back incomplete transactions using undo log records). ARIES guarantees that after recovery, the database reflects all committed transactions and none of the aborted ones.

runs.text: ARIES (Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics) is the foundational recovery algorithm. IBM DB2, SQL Server, and Postgres all implement ARIES or close derivatives. The key insight: it is safe to redo even uncommitted changes during crash recovery, because the subsequent undo phase will roll them back. This allows relaxed locking during recovery.

The transaction subsystem has three jobs: the transaction manager controls BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, the lock manager prevents conflicting concurrent access, and the recovery manager uses the WAL to ensure that crashes never leave the database in a half-written state.

cards.title: Query Subsystem — Parser, Planner, Optimizer, Executor
cards.teaser: A SQL query is a declarative statement: it says what you want, not how to get it. The query subsystem's job is to translate that declaration into an efficient sequence of operations — and that translation is where most of a database's observable performance lives.

runs.text: The query subsystem processes SQL in four stages:

items.text: Converts SQL text into a parse tree (abstract syntax tree). Validates syntax only — it does not check that the referenced tables or columns exist. Postgres's parser is generated from a yacc grammar and produces a
node tree. Parsing is cheap; query planning is not.
Resolves names to OIDs, expands views, checks permissions, and applies rewrite rules (e.g., rule-based view expansion in Postgres). Transforms the raw parse tree into a semantic

The most expensive and intellectually interesting stage. Takes the semantic query tree and enumerates possible execution plans — different join orders, different join algorithms (nested loop, hash join, merge join), different index access paths — then estimates the cost of each using table statistics (row counts, column histograms, correlation coefficients). Selects the plan with the lowest estimated cost. Postgres uses a dynamic programming optimizer for queries with up to
tables (default 8), then falls back to a genetic algorithm (GEQO) for larger queries. Bad statistics lead to bad plans;
Walks the plan tree using the Volcano/Iterator model (Graefe, 1990): each plan node implements

which pulls one row (or a batch in vectorized engines) from its children, applies its operator (filter, join, aggregate), and returns results upstream. The executor calls into the buffer pool to fetch pages and into the transaction subsystem to acquire row locks.

runs.text: The optimizer's cost model is only as good as the statistics it is given. Running VACUUM and ANALYZE regularly is not optional hygiene — it is the mechanism that keeps the optimizer's statistical model aligned with reality. A Postgres table that has grown 10× since its last ANALYZE will be planned as if it were small, leading to nested-loop joins on tables that need hash joins.

SQL is a wish list. The query subsystem turns that wish list into an execution plan in four steps: parse (check syntax), analyze (resolve names), optimize (pick the cheapest plan), execute (run it). The optimizer is where most query performance is won or lost.

cards.title: Buffer Pool Layer — The Bridge Between Disk and Memory
cards.teaser: The buffer pool is the most performance-critical subsystem in a disk-oriented database. Every page the executor reads, every row the lock manager examines, every WAL record the recovery manager writes — all of it flows through the buffer pool.

runs.text: The buffer pool is a region of shared memory subdivided into
frames
— each frame holds exactly one database page. It maintains a
page table

mapping page IDs to frame indices, plus metadata per frame: a dirty bit (page has been modified since read), a pin count (number of active users; pinned pages cannot be evicted), and access metadata for the replacement policy.

explanation.text:
Buffer pool structure:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           BUFFER POOL (shared memory)   │
  │                                         │
  │  Frame 0 │ Frame 1 │ Frame 2 │ ...      │
  │  page_42 │ page_7  │ (empty) │ ...      │
  │                                         │
  │  Page Table:                            │
  │    page_42 → frame 0, dirty=1, pins=1   │
  │    page_7  → frame 1, dirty=0, pins=0   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  On page request (page_99, not in pool):
  1. Choose victim frame (replacement policy)
  2. If victim is dirty → write to disk (eviction I/O)
  3. Read page_99 from disk into victim frame
  4. Update page table
  5. Pin frame, return pointer to caller

items.text: LRU (least recently used) is the classic choice — evict the page not accessed for the longest time. LRU-K improves on LRU by tracking the last K accesses, better handling sequential scans (which would pollute a pure LRU cache with one-time-use pages). Postgres uses a clock-sweep algorithm (a hardware-efficient approximation of LRU). InnoDB uses LRU with a midpoint insertion strategy to protect frequently accessed pages from sequential scan pollution.

Dirty pages must be written to disk before eviction. The checkpoint process periodically flushes dirty pages to reduce crash recovery time — the more dirty pages on disk, the shorter the WAL replay needed on restart. Postgres's bgwriter and checkpointer work together to spread this I/O over time rather than spiking it.
controls buffer pool size; the canonical starting point is 25% of RAM. InnoDB's
is typically set to 70–80% of RAM. Every cache miss is a disk I/O that costs microseconds to milliseconds — the buffer pool hit rate is one of the most important performance metrics in a DBMS.

runs.text: The buffer pool is a page cache in RAM. Every time the database needs a page, it checks the buffer pool first. If it is there, one memory read. If not, fetch from disk and cache it, possibly evicting an old page first. Keeping the hit rate high is the single most impactful tuning lever in any disk-based database.

cards.title: Disk-Oriented vs Memory-Oriented Databases — The Architectural Fork
cards.teaser: A disk-oriented database is designed with the assumption that the working set does not fit in RAM. A memory-oriented database (MMDB) assumes it does — and that assumption licenses a completely different architecture.

runs.text: For the first forty years of relational databases, RAM was the scarce resource and disk was the primary store. Architectures were built around minimizing disk I/O at every level — the buffer pool, B-tree page splits, WAL fsync ordering, even query plan selection. Every major decision in Postgres and InnoDB reflects this constraint.
Today, a server with 3 TB of RAM is commercially available. For workloads where the entire hot dataset fits in memory, the entire disk-oriented architecture becomes overhead:

items.text: If all data lives in RAM, there is no concept of a cache miss or a page eviction. An MMDB can use direct memory addressing rather than indirection through a page table. VoltDB, H-Store, and Redis eliminate the buffer pool entirely.

Pages exist because disks read in sectors — a constraint that disappears when data lives in RAM. MMDBs can use pointer-based data structures (linked lists, skip lists, hash tables, tries) that would be catastrophically slow on disk due to random access patterns.
Volatility is the price of RAM. A power failure loses everything not written to persistent storage. MMDBs use WAL or snapshots to ensure durability, but the WAL is the
I/O bottleneck — not page reads or buffer pool eviction. Redis's AOF (append-only file) and RDB snapshots serve this role.

Without disk I/O latency, the cost of holding a lock changes. VoltDB uses a partitioned, single-threaded execution model per partition, eliminating locking overhead entirely by serializing access to each partition's data. H-Store pioneered this "no locks needed" architecture.

runs.text: Buffer pool essential
Fixed-size pages
B-tree favored for cache efficiency
WAL + data page I/O both on critical path
No buffer pool
Pointer-based structures
Skip lists, hash tables viable
Only WAL I/O on critical path

A disk-oriented database is designed to work when most data is on disk and only a fraction fits in RAM. A memory-oriented database assumes everything fits in RAM and throws away the page-cache machinery that exists solely to hide disk latency.

cards.title: Embedded vs Client-Server — When Each Fits
cards.teaser: SQLite and Postgres represent two fundamentally different deployment models for a relational database. Choosing the wrong model produces either unnecessary operational overhead or unacceptable performance cliffs.

runs.text: The
client-server

model — exemplified by Postgres, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server — runs the database engine as a long-lived daemon process. Client applications connect over a TCP socket (or Unix domain socket), send SQL text, and receive result sets. The database server manages a shared buffer pool, a lock manager for concurrent clients, and a WAL writer — all of which survive across connections.
The
embedded

model — exemplified by SQLite, DuckDB, and LMDB — links the database engine as a library directly into the application process. There is no daemon, no TCP socket, no separate process. The application calls into the engine via a function call, and the engine reads and writes files in the same process address space.

items.text: a single process owns the data (mobile apps, desktop apps, CLI tools, in-process caches, test suites). SQLite is the most deployed database in the world by instance count — every iPhone, every Android device, every browser runs SQLite. DuckDB is rapidly becoming the embedded OLAP equivalent for data-science workflows.

multiple processes or machines need concurrent access to the same data, when the database must outlive any single application process, or when the working set requires centralized shared memory management. Web applications with connection pools, microservice architectures, and multi-tenant SaaS products all require the client-server model.

SQLite serializes all writes using a process-level write lock on the database file. Multiple concurrent writers stall. This is fine for a single-user application; it is catastrophic for a web server with hundreds of concurrent requests. Attempting to use SQLite as a client-server replacement is the classic embedded-vs-client-server mistake.

runs.text: SQLite's author, D. Richard Hipp, describes SQLite as "a serverless, zero-configuration, transactional SQL database engine." The critical word is serverless — not in the cloud-functions sense, but in the literal sense: no server process. SQLite in WAL mode supports one writer concurrently with multiple readers, but still serializes writers.

Embedded databases (SQLite, DuckDB) run inside your application process — no server, no TCP connection. Client-server databases (Postgres, MySQL) run as separate daemons that multiple clients share. Choose embedded when one process owns the data; choose client-server when multiple processes or machines need concurrent access.

cards.title: Row-Store vs Column-Store — Physical Layout Consequences
cards.teaser: Row-oriented and column-oriented storage are not just different serialization formats — they produce fundamentally different I/O access patterns, compression ratios, and CPU utilization profiles. The right choice depends entirely on the read/write mix.

runs.text: In a
row-oriented store

(NSM — N-ary Storage Model), all columns of a single row are stored contiguously on disk. Reading a row is a single I/O; writing a row is a single I/O. Updating a row touches at most one page. This is optimal for OLTP workloads dominated by primary-key lookups and single-row updates.
In a
column-oriented store

(DSM — Decomposition Storage Model), each column is stored as a contiguous sequence across all rows. A query reading only three of fifty columns loads only those three column files — 3/50 = 6% of the I/O of the equivalent row scan. For OLAP queries that aggregate over millions of rows but touch only a handful of attributes, this is a decisive advantage.

items.text: Columns contain homogeneous values (same type, often same domain). Dictionary encoding, run-length encoding, and delta encoding all exploit this — a "country" column with 200 distinct values compresses 100–300× with dictionary encoding. Row stores compress poorly because adjacent bytes are type-heterogeneous.

Column chunks load naturally into CPU vector registers. DuckDB and ClickHouse process column batches of 1024–2048 values per SIMD instruction, achieving throughput unreachable by row-at-a-time engines.

Inserting a single row in a column store requires writing N column files — one per column. This is write amplification at the storage model level. Column stores mitigate this with write-buffer batching: accumulate inserts in a row-oriented buffer (like an LSM-tree memtable), then flush as column-oriented compressed blocks.

runs.text: Row stores pack all columns of a row together — fast for single-row reads and writes. Column stores pack all values of one column together — fast for analytical queries that scan a few columns across many rows. The choice commits your engine to very different I/O, compression, and CPU characteristics.

cards.title: OLTP vs OLAP — Why the Same Engine Struggles with Both
cards.teaser: OLTP and OLAP workloads are not just different in scale — they impose contradictory physical design requirements. Understanding the tension explains why nearly every serious data platform ends up with separate systems.

runs.text: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) workloads are characterized by short, concurrent transactions each touching a small number of rows. The canonical OLTP query: find order #4827, update its status, return the result. This requires:

items.text: — read and write entire rows efficiently.
— row-level locks so thousands of concurrent transactions don't block each other.

runs.text: OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) workloads are characterized by long-running queries scanning billions of rows to compute aggregates. The canonical OLAP query: total revenue by product category and region for Q3 over 500 million order rows. This requires:

items.text: — read only the columns in the query's projection and WHERE clause.
— skip entire column segments outside the query's filter range.
— process column batches with SIMD instructions.
— no point lookups; read everything, compress everything.

runs.text: The conflict is fundamental: an engine optimized for row-oriented point reads cannot efficiently do column-oriented scans, and vice versa. Postgres added columnar extensions (TimescaleDB, Citus columnar) and parallel sequential scan, but it remains a row store at heart. ClickHouse is a ferociously fast OLAP engine that is painful to use for high-concurrency OLTP.

The HTAP (Hybrid Transaction/Analytical Processing) effort — embodied by TiDB, SingleStore (MemSQL), and CockroachDB with follower reads — attempts to serve both from one system. The usual approach: maintain a row store for OLTP writes and a column store replica for OLAP reads, replicating between them. The two stores are fundamentally separate; the HTAP label describes the replication plumbing.

Running analytics directly against a production OLTP database is the most common database performance mistake. A long-running GROUP BY scan acquires shared locks (or degrades concurrent writes via buffer pool pollution), directly impacting online users. The correct solution is a read replica or a separate OLAP system — not a bigger OLTP server.

OLTP is many short transactions each touching one or a few rows. OLAP is a few long queries each scanning billions of rows. The storage layout, indexes, locking model, and CPU execution strategy each workload needs are almost perfectly opposite — which is why they end up on different systems.

cards.title: Storage Hierarchy — Latency at Every Level
cards.teaser: Database performance is ultimately constrained by the storage hierarchy. Every design decision in a DBMS — from B-tree page size to buffer pool replacement policy — is an attempt to exploit faster levels of the hierarchy and avoid slower ones.

runs.text: The storage hierarchy is a physical law, not a design choice. Every computer has multiple tiers of storage, each larger and slower than the one above it:

explanation.text:
Storage Hierarchy — approximate latencies (2024 hardware)

  Level              Size        Latency        Bandwidth
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  CPU Registers      ~1 KB       0.25 ns        ~TB/s
  L1 Cache           32–64 KB    ~1 ns           ~1 TB/s
  L2 Cache           256 KB–1 MB ~4 ns           ~400 GB/s
  L3 Cache           6–60 MB     ~10 ns          ~200 GB/s
  DRAM (RAM)         GBs–TBs     ~60–100 ns      ~50–100 GB/s
  NVMe SSD           TBs         ~100 µs         ~7 GB/s
  SATA SSD           TBs         ~500 µs         ~500 MB/s
  HDD (spinning)     TBs         ~5–10 ms        ~100–200 MB/s
  Network (LAN)      —           ~100 µs–1 ms    ~1–100 GB/s
  Network (WAN/S3)   —           ~10–100 ms      ~1–10 GB/s
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Ratio: HDD random read ≈ 40,000,000× slower than L1 cache

runs.text: These numbers make specific DBMS design choices immediately legible:

items.text: because DRAM access (60 ns) is ~100,000× faster than HDD random access (5–10 ms). Fitting the working set in RAM turns catastrophic I/O into trivial cache hits.
because at 500 children per node, a billion-row table needs only 4 levels. Upper levels are permanently hot in the buffer pool, reducing the median read to 1–2 disk I/Os.

because HDDs deliver ~200 MB/s sequentially but only ~100–200 random reads per second (5–10 ms per seek). SSDs narrow this gap but do not eliminate it — NAND write amplification still rewards sequential writes.

adds a new tier: larger than local disk, but with latency in the milliseconds range for metadata operations and first-byte reads. Cloud databases like Aurora and Neon separate compute from storage, placing shared storage on a distributed network layer — trading local-disk latency for elastic capacity.

runs.text: Every level of storage in a computer is faster but smaller than the level below it. A CPU register is a million times faster than a spinning disk. Every database design decision — caching, page size, sequential writes — is an attempt to keep hot data in the faster levels and avoid falling to the slow ones.

cards.title: Read Amplification — More Bytes Read Than Logically Required
cards.teaser: Read amplification is the ratio of bytes read from storage to bytes of user data returned. An amplification factor of 10 means the database reads 10 bytes of physical data for every 1 byte the query needed. It is the hidden tax on every read path.

runs.text: Read amplification arises from two independent sources:
storage structure overhead
and
unnecessary column or page reads

items.text: Fetching a single row from a B-tree index requires reading from root to leaf — typically 3–5 page reads for a million-row table. Only the leaf page contains user data; the internal pages are structural overhead. For a 4 KB leaf on an 8 KB page, the read amplification just from tree traversal is (3 × 8 KB) / (row size). For small rows (100 bytes), RA from B-tree traversal alone is ~240×.

Without Bloom filters, an LSM read must probe the memtable and every SSTable level. With 6 levels, that is up to 6 disk reads for a key that exists, and 6 reads to confirm a non-existent key. Bloom filters reduce this to near 1, but the theoretical RA of a naïve LSM is O(number of levels).

A SELECT on 3 columns of a 100-column table in a row store reads all 100 columns to deliver 3 — a 33× read amplification at the page level. Column stores eliminate this by reading only the requested column files.

In Postgres, older row versions are stored in the heap alongside live tuples. A long-running transaction that reads rows modified by many other transactions must follow MVCC version chains to find the visible version — reading more data than the current logical state requires. This is why VACUUM (which prunes dead tuples) matters for read performance, not just storage.

runs.text: Read amplification is measured empirically using tools like iostat, pg_statio_all_tables, or RocksDB's perf_context. A buffer pool hit-rate close to 100% masks high read amplification in production — the amplification only becomes visible when the working set exceeds buffer pool size and cold data flows off the cache.

Read amplification is how much extra data the database has to read to answer a query. If you ask for one row and the database reads ten pages to find it, your read amplification is high. Column stores, Bloom filters, and good buffer pool management all exist to reduce it.

cards.title: Write Amplification — More Bytes Written Than Logically Required
cards.teaser: Write amplification is the ratio of bytes written to storage to bytes of user data written. It is the dominant cost in write-heavy workloads and a significant contributor to SSD wear. Every write path in a database — WAL, B-tree, LSM-tree — has a characteristic amplification factor.

runs.text: Write amplification (WA) compounds at multiple layers of the stack. A single logical write can trigger writes at the WAL layer, the page layer, the compaction layer, and even the SSD's internal flash translation layer:

items.text: Every database write is written twice: once to the WAL (sequential, append-only), and once to the data page (random). This baseline WA of 2× is universal in WAL-based systems. InnoDB's doublewrite buffer adds a third write for torn-page protection.

Updating one row in a B-tree requires reading the leaf page, modifying it in the buffer pool, and writing the entire 8 KB or 16 KB page back to disk — even if the row is 50 bytes. For a 50-byte row in a 16 KB page, the physical WA from B-tree page writes alone is 16,384 / 50 = 327×. This is mitigated by batching: many rows are modified per page flush.

Leveled compaction in RocksDB cascades a key's data through each level as compaction fires. Petrov (2019) measures typical leveled compaction WA at 10–30×. For an SSD rated at 1 DWPD (drive writes per day), a 10× WA means your application can only write at 1/10 the device's rated throughput before exceeding its wear budget.

NAND flash cannot overwrite in place — it must erase entire blocks (512 KB–4 MB) before writing. The SSD's FTL performs its own internal WA to manage garbage collection of erased blocks. A database with high random write WA will drive FTL WA even higher, accelerating SSD wear and reducing sustained write throughput.

runs.text: Write amplification stacks multiplicatively: if WAL contributes 2×, compaction contributes 10×, and FTL contributes 5×, the total physical WA against the SSD is 2 × 10 × 5 = 100×. A 1 KB user write results in 100 KB of physical NAND writes. This is why write-heavy workloads at scale are bottlenecked on storage throughput even with NVMe SSDs.

Write amplification is how many bytes hit disk for every byte you logically wrote. The WAL doubles every write. B-tree page writes rewrite an entire 16 KB page for a 50-byte update. LSM compaction rewrites data many times across levels. These multiply together — and all of it accelerates SSD wear.

cards.title: Space Amplification — Storage Overhead Beyond Logical Data Size
cards.teaser: Space amplification is the ratio of bytes consumed on disk to bytes of live logical data. A space amplification of 3 means the database uses 3 GB of storage for every 1 GB of user data. It accrues from indexing, versioning, fragmentation, and compaction lag.

runs.text: Space amplification is the least dramatic of the three amplification factors — it does not affect query latency directly. But it compounds into real cost at scale: a 10× space amplification on a 10 TB logical dataset requires 100 TB of storage, with corresponding IOPS and throughput costs.

items.text: Every secondary index duplicates the indexed columns plus a primary key pointer. A table with 10 secondary indexes on wide columns can use 3–5× the storage of the raw data. Partial indexes (Postgres
clause on index) and expression indexes help, but index count remains the dominant SA driver in OLTP schemas.

Postgres's MVCC writes new row versions in-place in the heap without immediately discarding old versions. A UPDATE-heavy workload (e.g., a counter column incremented every second) can accumulate thousands of dead tuple versions per row. Until VACUUM removes them, they occupy disk space and inflate heap file size. A table that is UPDATE-heavy but VACUUM-light will grow without bound even if the logical data size is constant.

With size-tiered compaction (Cassandra's default), multiple tiers of SSTables coexist. Before compaction fires, you may have 2–3× the logical data size on disk across all tiers. Leveled compaction keeps SA closer to 1.1× because each level is size-bounded.

After many insertions and deletions, B-tree leaf pages accumulate holes (from deleted or updated rows) that cannot be filled by new inserts without reorganization. Postgres's VACUUM FULL rewrites a table into a compact B-tree;
does the same online. Without periodic defragmentation, a heavily updated table can use 2–4× its logical size in pages.

runs.text: Space amplification is the silent killer of database budgets. The table that looked like 500 GB two years ago is now 6 TB because nobody ran VACUUM, dead tuples accumulated, and MVCC chains grew without bound. Always monitor table bloat (pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup in Postgres) and SSTable count alongside the logical data size.

Space amplification is how much storage you use vs. how much live data you have. Indexes duplicate data. Dead MVCC tuples stick around until vacuumed. LSM tiers hold multiple copies during compaction. B-tree pages have holes after deletes. All of it adds up — sometimes by a factor of 10 or more.

cards.title: The RUM Conjecture — Pick Any Two
cards.teaser: The RUM conjecture (Athanassoulis et al., CIDR 2016) states that no access method can simultaneously minimize Read amplification, Update (write) amplification, and Memory (space) amplification. It is the fundamental trilemma of database design.

runs.text: Manos Athanassoulis and colleagues formalized the RUM conjecture in the paper
Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture
(CIDR 2016). The paper proves that for any access method, reducing two of the three amplification factors forces an increase in the third. The three factors are:

items.text: Extra reads performed per logical read.
Extra writes performed per logical write.
Extra storage used per byte of logical data.

runs.text: The conjecture positions every real-world storage engine on this triangle:

explanation.text:
Minimize Read Amplification
                    R
                   /|\
                  / | \
                 /  |  \
        B-tree  /   |   \  
               /    |    \   
              /     |     \  
            U───────────────M
   Minimize              Minimize
   Write Ampl.           Space Ampl.
   (LSM-tree)            (sorted array)

Examples:
  B-tree:             Low R, low M, moderate U
  LSM (size-tiered):  Low U, moderate R, high M
  LSM (leveled):      Low M, moderate R, high U
  Sorted array:       Low R, low M, very high U (writes resort everything)
  Hash index:         Near-zero R, low U, high M (no range queries)

runs.text: The practical consequences of the RUM conjecture:

items.text: B-trees optimize for low R and low M
at the cost of moderate U (WAL double-write, page overwrites, page splits). This is why B-trees dominate read-heavy OLTP workloads.
LSM-trees with leveled compaction optimize for low M and acceptable R
at the cost of high U (10–30× write amplification from cascading compaction). This is why RocksDB dominates write-heavy OLTP workloads.
LSM-trees with size-tiered compaction optimize for low U
at the cost of higher R (more SSTables to probe) and higher M (more tiers coexisting). This is Cassandra's default — appropriate for write-heavy, storage-plentiful deployments.
No engine can be globally optimal.

A vendor claiming their database is fastest for reads, writes, and uses the least storage is either lying or measuring a specialized workload. The RUM conjecture says that claim is physically impossible in general.

runs.text: The RUM conjecture is not a proof that you cannot improve all three simultaneously for a specific workload — it is a proof that no access method can universally minimize all three. Real engines make explicit trade-off choices (leveled vs size-tiered; B-tree vs LSM) based on the target workload. Understanding which vertex of the RUM triangle a given engine favors tells you immediately where its performance cliffs are.

The RUM conjecture says: for any storage engine, you can minimize reads, minimize writes, or minimize space — but not all three simultaneously. Every database engine is a specific trade-off on this triangle. B-trees trade writes for fast reads. LSM-trees trade reads for fast writes. Knowing which trade-off an engine made tells you exactly what its limits are.
